CausalChain: EMT in tumor cells -> Increased release of IL-6–rich exosomes -> Uptake by distant stromal/immune cells -> IL-6 receptor engagement -> JAK2 activation -> STAT3 phosphorylation -> Upregulation of pro-survival, EMT, and immunosuppressive genes -> Establishment of a pre-metastatic niche and chemoresistance
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived exosomes, carrying IL-6, mediate the propagation of the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling cascade across distant microenvironments, leading to the formation of a pre-metastatic niche that enhances cancer metastasis and drug resistance.
Abstract: We propose that tumor-derived exosomes serve as active vehicles for IL-6, thereby extending and amplifying the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling axis beyond the primary tumor microenvironment. In this model, cancer cells that undergo epithelial‐to‐mesenchymal transition (EMT) release exosomes enriched in IL-6 mRNA and/or protein. When taken up by distal stromal cells such as fibroblasts or resident immune cells, these exosomes trigger IL-6 receptor engagement, leading to JAK2 phosphorylation and subsequent STAT3 activation. This process drives the transcription of genes involved in cell survival, EMT, and immunosuppression, establishing a pre‐metastatic niche that favors tumor dissemination and chemoresistance. Therefore, targeting either the exosomal packaging or the exosome‐mediated transfer of IL‐6 may provide a novel therapeutic route to disrupt the metastatic cascade.
